text:
maria-support: FYI escalation from AcmeCorp — they're hitting persistent 429s on their Dedicated reserved pool during a nightly batch. They say capacity was reserved but tokens got exhausted and 429s kept returning even after traffic dropped. @alex-sre can you triage?

alex-sre: Thanks. Can you paste the response headers from a failing request and the reserved_pool_id + config (headroom/commit)? Also what endpoint were they streaming vs non-streaming?

maria-support: Headers pasted from customer (redacted):
```
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
X-RateLimit-Limit: 200
X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0
X-RateLimit-Reset: 1714209900
Retry-After: 30
X-Reserved-Pool-ID: rp-58d3a1
X-Pool-Headroom: 5%\n```
They were calling /v1/generate with streaming (chunked SSE) from a batch runner. They reported a spike at 10:03 UTC and then 429s for ~12 minutes even though overall QPS dropped.

ben-eng: Looks like the reserved pool's token bucket hit zero and entered a penalty window — the Retry-After aligns with short penalty backoff. Streaming connections can hold onto resources longer (active KV cache, open streams) and if the pool's burst credits were already low, a flood of long-lived streams will deplete burst credit faster than refill.

jess-support: From customer notes: they spawn ~5k parallel streaming workers during the batch (each opens a stream and keeps it for 90-120s while consuming tokens). The batch runs for ~2 hours. They expected the reserved pool to cover the spike because they purchased Dedicated capacity.

alex-sre: Two quick asks to repro: 1) a curl example of the streaming call (headers + body), 2) the dedicated config for rp-58d3a1 (committed qps, headroom %, autoscale/burst settings). If we can reproduce with a local stress run we can confirm burst-credit depletion vs auth/handshake drift.

maria-support: curl they used (simplified):
```
curl -N -H "Authorization: Bearer <KEY>" \
  -H "Accept: text/event-stream" \
  -d '{"model":"insta-large","stream":true,"max_tokens":1024}' \
  https://api.redwood.example/v1/generate
```
Config snippet from console (customer): committed qps: 180, autoscale burst: enabled, headroom: 5% (UI).

ben-eng: Repro plan I ran locally to simulate: spin up 1k concurrent short-lived streaming clients that each pull ~900 tokens over 90s. With headroom=5% and commit close to observed peak, the token bucket fell to zero within ~3 minutes and the pool hit a penalty window — subsequent requests (even after QPS drop) got 429s until the bucket refilled.

ben-eng: Key root causes we saw in repro: 
- Small headroom (5%) + many long-lived streams = burst-credit depletion.
- Streaming requests consume tokens as they arrive; open streams keep KV and scheduling slots busy which reduces effective throughput and delays refill.
- The per-VM token accounting can mean a global-looking reserved pool still shows short-term exhaustion if many streams target the same serving shard.

alex-sre: Short-term mitigations to propose to AcmeCorp: 
- Increase reserved pool headroom to 15-25% as a quick stopgap.
- Temporarily raise committed capacity or enable extra burst capacity for the next batch window.
- Add client-side rate shaping: limit concurrent streams, or batch requests into fewer connections.
- Implement exponential backoff on 429 with jitter for reconnects so they don't thrash the pool.

ryan-platform: We can also provision a temporary burst allocation on their Dedicated cluster for the next run — but we need approval from billing (this will change committed usage). Note on SLA: Dedicated SLOs assume customers stay within committed qps + configured headroom. Persistent overcommit without increased reservation isn't covered by SLA.

jess-support: Customer asked whether this is an auth issue or billing mismatch. Which is it?

ben-eng: Not auth. Headers show token accounting was exhausted. Billing/commit mismatch only if their sustained QPS exceeds the committed qps — here it's a burst profile (short window of many streams). Billing won't auto-cover burst unless they increase commit or buy burst add-ons.

alex-sre: Long-term fix suggestions we should include in the postmortem: 
- Recommend scheduling large streaming batches during off-peak windows or splitting across multiple pool IDs/regions to avoid shard hot-spotting.
- Tune autoscale burst policy to prefer short-lived worker pools for streaming workloads (lower connection lifetime).
- Consider enabling server-side prefix/KV caching for their repeated prompt patterns to cut token load.
- Add a proactive alert: reserved_pool_remaining_percentage < 10% for > 1m during a reserved job => notify SE + customer.

maria-support: I'll draft the customer-facing notes: explanation, short-term options (headroom bump + temp burst), and long-term recommendations. Schedule call with AcmeCorp for tomorrow 09:00 PT.

sre-bot: Incident INC-2026-1234 created, assigned to alex-sre, priority P2.

jess-support: Thanks team — will send summary to customer now :thumbsup:
